Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters View image in fullscreen Ken Martin, chair of the Democratic National Committee, during a campaign rally for Mikie Sherrill in Newark, New Jersey, on 1 November 2025. Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters Democrats Author of Democrats’ 2024 election autopsy report says chapter was left out Paul Rivera says missing section included questions on Biden’s decision to run for re-election, the Times reports Edward Helmore Mon 3 Aug 2026 13.33 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 14.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The author of an infamous internal Democrat party report on the 2024 presidential election loss has claimed that an entire section that included a discussion of generational wealth established by high-ranking elected officials was cut from the draft version leaked and later released earlier this summer. Paul Rivera, the author of the autopsy, told the New York Times that a section titled “What Happened in 2024” was missing from the published version but had been included in the version he personally handed to embattled party chairman, Ken Martin, in January. The Democratic National Committee has previously claimed the autopsy had been released “ in its entirety ”. Rivera said that elements of the report that were excised included questions about Joe Biden’s decision to run for re-election and the policy influence of Democrat party operatives who had become “generationally wealthy off politics”. While the chapter did not name those who had become enriched he wrote that Democrats seeking change “keep banging their heads up against a system proven to be inflexible and self-enriching. “Whether that was a conscious decision on their part to bury the section for the purposes of hiding a paragraph, I don’t know,” Rivera told the Times. “That’s a them question. What I can tell you is they had it, and they made a decision not to release it.” Martin disputed that account in statement to the paper, saying “this alleged report section was not in any binder I reviewed”. Had it been included, he added, “we would have released it with the rest of the report.” The report was released in May to resounding disappointment that it had failed to address why the party, or its two presidential candidates, Biden and later Vice-President Kamala Harris, had failed to gain sufficient traction to win against Donald Trump. The missing chapter, provided by Rivera and published in full by the Times , states that Democratic wins before the election led the party “to believe they were stronger than they actually were. President Biden, seeing those results, made the consequential decision to seek re-election even when Americans were already sending a very strong signal: they were unhappy with the status quo.” The report said that Democrats had failed to do enough to convince voters that Trump was an unacceptable candidate and made wrong assumptions about Latino and male voters. It pointed to successful Democratic candidates in swing states who concentrated on economic and cost-of-living messaging more than identity politics. The Democrat party now heads into the midterm elections in November and the 2028 presidential election with a significant $2m cash deficit while the Republican party nationally reports a positive balance over $128m. A recent supreme court decision indicates that the cash gap could widen. Among the topics Rivera attempted to address in the disputed “What Happened” chapter were entries about Biden’s decision to seek re-election; a loss of support among Hispanic, Black, Asian American and Native American voters; and the issue of party officials and consultants being insulated or divorced from voters’ concerns by wealth. “It is therefore possible the people ‘in the room’ at the highest levels of 2024 decision making misunderstood the mood and practicalities facing everyday America,” Rivera wrote, according to the missing section. “They missed important signals about why people were frustrated with Democrats, who seemed not to appreciate or understand their situation.” The Times report may now set off a new round of questions about its direction as Democratic primary voters head to the polls in Michigan on Tuesday to choose between moderate and progressive Senate candidates Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed. Martin said the party would have released the disputed or missing chapter “that went after self-enriching consultants” if it had had them and that he personally had campaigned for the party chairmanship “to hold the consultant-industrial complex accountable and ensure the party only pays for work that actually helps us win”. Rivera said he was now going public with the claim, along with his own 564-page review of the election loss. “It’s coming from a place of hope and, honestly, a little bit of desperation,” he told the outlet. “I think that we need some disruption here to force change.” Explore more on these topics Democrats US elections 2024 US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed

Photograph: Skanda Gautam/SOPA Images/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen The aftermath of the floods in Nuwakot, Nepal. More than 1,300 people are missing. Photograph: Skanda Gautam/SOPA Images/Shutterstock Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Race to get aid into Nepal and Tibet amid warnings flood lake could burst Flash floods have killed at least 359 people while homes and infrastructure have been swept away Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates What caused the flash flood in Nepal and Tibet? Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Kathmandu, Sam Jones and Amy Hawkins Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.22 EDT Last modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.54 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The international community was scrambling to get aid into flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet on Thursday as authorities warned that a lake ⁠formed at the ⁠site ⁠where the ​deadly torrents occurred ⁠was rising and ⁠at risk ​of ‌bursting. The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and obliterating entire villages, killed at least 359 people and left more than 1,300 missing. Efforts to locate those unaccounted for – including hundreds of tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada – have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and 25 miles (40km) of roads in the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims. Satellite images showing before and after collapse Rescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters. Videos from Wednesday’s disaster showed a massive wall of water crashing down on the border as people tried to flee. The power, volume and speed of the floods gave little time for escape. Trucks were overturned and houses, roads ⁠and power plants were swept away in Nepal, while ​officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties” after a mudslide hit a border crossing. How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guide Read more Tom Fletcher, the UN’s humanitarian chief, described the flood as “horrifying”. He said emergency teams had been mobilised and an initial $2m (£1.5m) of disaster funds allocated to cover emergency medical care, shelter and water. 9:21 ‘Tsunami from the sky:’ floods leave trail of devastation in Nepal and Tibet - The Latest Nepal’s disaster authority warned of continuing danger on Thursday, appealing to residents and rescuers to stay away from a swelling lake that had formed at the flood site. Chinese authorities said a barrier lake at the confluence of the Tsogyal and Purupqiangzangbu rivers was overflowing and could burst. Girilal Budhathoki, 36, who lives in the Rasuwa district of Nepal’s Bagmati province, said the flood waters swept away his wife and four children while he was away from the family home. “A huge surge of water came,” he said. “Everything turned completely black, and I couldn’t understand what was happening. Suddenly, something heavy crushed me and I fell down.” Budhathoki realised what had happened only when he returned to the place where his house had stood. “I searched desperately for my wife and children but I couldn’t find them,” he said. “They didn’t make it out. My wife was swept away too. I am all alone now.” Map Kamal Kharel, who works at a hydropower plant in Chilime, also in Rasuwa district, was in the office when the floods hit. “The whole place shook as if there had been a huge earthquake,” he said. “But when I went outside, I saw everything a storm and raging water.” Kharel and some of his colleagues managed to climb a hill, where they stayed until they were rescued by the army on Thursday morning. He said: “I had never seen waves crashing that high. You only see waves like that in the sea.” People from the hard-hit districts of Nuwakot and Dhading, in Bagmati province, were seen gathering outside an army training centre – the base for helicopter rescue operations – seeking information about missing family members. Police were recording the names of the missing outside the barracks gate. Mobile phone torches were their only source of light as the area remained without electricity because of damaged hydroelectric infrastructure. View image in fullscreen Flooding has caused widespread damage to homes, roads, bridges and other infrastructure in Nuwakot, Nepal. Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/Zuma Press/Shutterstock The village of Soley, in Nuwakot, which had about 25 homes, was almost wiped out, according to Nirajan Paudyal, a Kathmandu-based journalist whose parents and other relatives lived there. Desperate for information, he had travelled to the area on Thursday for news of his family. “There is no update till now,” he said. “I fear there won’t be any update.” More than 500 foreigners were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said. Among those unaccounted for were 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada. Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals. Police in Nepal said 359 ⁠bodies had been recovered by Thursday afternoon local time, while Chinese state media reported three dead on the Tibet side of the border. Many of the victims were on a pilgrimage to Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists among others. Early reports from Nepali ​officials suggested an earthquake could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger ‌the floods. But the US Geological Survey later said what was initially reported ‌as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake was a seismic shock generated by glacial rock and ice collapsing, and the flow of debris. “No earthquake had occurred,” it said. A graphic showing how the situation unfolded. Srijana Gurung, the acting Nepal director for the international NGO Plan International, said communities across the Himalayan country were facing “climate shock after shock” with hardly any time to recover. “Floods and landslides have always happened in Nepal but the climate crisis is making them far more frequent and intense,” she said. “The priority now must be reaching those affected, supporting families searching for loved ones and ensuring vulnerable communities have the assistance they need.” Gurung said children and families who had lost their homes and livelihoods would be in urgent need of medical help, food, shelter and hygiene kits. “There is also a risk of waterborne disease as access to clean water and sanitation is likely to have been damaged,” she said. View image in fullscreen People look at the devastation left by flash flooding in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Scant information has emerged from the Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction. Tibet is the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Foreign journalists cannot visit the region unless they are part of a government-controlled tour and the authorities have cracked down harshly on calls for greater autonomy from the Tibetan people. Tibetans have almost no contact with the international media because of fears of retribution. Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts. Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch, wrote on X: “The floods raise questions about whether Chinese authorities could’ve done more to reduce disaster risks, given longstanding concerns from Tibetan diaspora groups & experts about rapid, state-led development in areas where Tibetans have little say.” She called on Beijing to “allow Tibetans access to information and international researchers and journalists unfettered access to the region, and conduct a rigorous investigation into the disaster”. Israeli strikes hit Gaza shelters, killing four amid deteriorating camp conditions Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 28/08/2026 - 17:17 GMT+2 Israeli strikes killed at least four people in Gaza, hitting a tent shelter and worsening conditions in overcrowded camps plagued by pests and poor sanitation. … More At least four people were killed in Israeli strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday, according to local health officials. Three men died in separate strikes in Gaza City, with their bodies taken to Shifa Hospital, while another person was killed when a tent sheltering displaced Palestinians was hit in southern Gaza. Several others were injured. Israel’s military said the strikes targeted Hamas militants. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT The attacks came as Palestinians continued to live in makeshift shelters after months of war and repeated displacement. In Gaza City, displaced resident Mohammad Hamad said on 27 August that people remained afraid to let their children outside and questioned whether the ceasefire was holding. Conditions are also deteriorating in overcrowded displacement camps. Footage filmed in Khan Younis in August showed displaced families dealing with rats, scorpions and other pests amid damaged sanitation systems and piles of rubble. The United Nations said in April that rodents and other pests were frequently observed at 80 per cent of displacement sites. https://www.irishtimes.com/culture/books.text: Subscriber Only Books Review Paul Celan: A Life: magisterial biography makes for essential reading Anna Arno examines the life and work of the man who wrote some of the greatest poetry of the 20th century Poet Paul Celan wanted to push language to its limits to say the unspeakable. Photogaph: Ullstein Bild via Getty Michael O'Loughlin Sat Sept 05 2026 - 04:16 • 2 MIN READ Paul Celan: A Life Author : Anna Arno, tr. Soren Gauger ISBN-13 : 978-0674298637 Publisher : Harvard University Press Guideline Price : £29.95; 384pp Paul Celan was born in 1920 to a German-speaking Jewish family in what had until recently been the city of Czernowitz, on the edge of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. By then it had become part of Romania, known as Cernauti. After the second World War it became part of the Soviet Union, and is now the Ukrainian city of Chernivtsi. Celan went to Hebrew school, spoke Romanian and learned French and Russian. But German was the language in which he would write some of the greatest poetry of the 20 th century. During the war the Nazis murdered and deported many of the Jews in Chernivtsi, including Celan’s family. He survived by hiding in a labour camp. His relationship with German was complex. After all, as he pointed out, his mother tongue had murdered his mother. After the war he went to Bucharest and started his literary career. In 1947 people smugglers helped him across the border and he reached Vienna, where he met many German-language writers, and published in German. But Paris was his destination, and he got there in 1949. It would be his home for the next 20 years. Celan’s early work was criticised for being hermetic and difficult. But Celan insisted that he was a realist. The apparent difficulty arose from his attempt to push language to its limits to say the unspeakable. In his most famous poem, Deathfugue, he writes: “ ... as smoke you’ll rise on the air/then you’ll have a grave in the sky.” As Anna Arno acutely points out, this is not a metaphor. Ourselves Alone: Sinn Féin Behind Closed Doors by Siobhán Fenton Despite this, his work would later be acclaimed in Germany, and he visited it often for readings and awards. But he was never at home in what he called “the land of the perpetrators”. His final years in Paris were difficult. He was hospitalised for long periods after psychotic episodes and eventually took his own life in the Seine on April 20th, 1970. This magisterial biography was written in Polish, and this background gives Arno special insights into the complexities of the eastern European bloodlands, and it is unlikely to be bettered. It is an essential introduction to the poetry of a man who is now seen as one of the big figures of the 20th century.
